Strata Marcella
STRAH-tuh mar-SEL-uh
n. (a Cistercian abbey near Welshpool in Powys, founded 1170 by Owain Cyfeiliog; it had the largest Cistercian church in Wales and almost nothing of it survives)
Latin strata Marcella, the Latin rendering of the Welsh Ystrad Marchell, the vale of Marchell.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Strata Marcella was founded in 1170 by Owain Cyfeiliog, prince of Powys, a daughter of Whitland, and its church was the largest the Cistercians ever raised in Wales. Owain himself took the habit there and died a monk. Today there is a field. Excavation in the nineteenth century found the foundations and a scatter of carved stone; the fabric went into farm buildings and the river took the rest. The abbey is therefore the strongest possible illustration of a verse that was written about men and applies without alteration to their works: “For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more” (Psa 103:16). The Psalmist is not being bleak. He sets that sentence beside the mercy that “is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him” (Psa 103:17), and the contrast is the point of the whole psalm. A prince who ended his days as a monk in the greatest church in Wales, and whose church is now pasture, has preached the first half; whether he believed the second half is between him and God, but the dictionary may say this much: the grass is the honest part. “As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines ruin as the remains of a decayed or demolished city, house or fortress; and perish as to die, to lose life in any manner, to be destroyed, to come to nothing.

expand to see more

RUIN, n. Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat. The remains of a decayed or demolished city, house, fortress, or any work of men.

PERISH, v.i. To die; to lose life in any manner; to be destroyed; to come to nothing.

GRASS, n. In common usage, herbage; the plants which constitute the food of cattle and other beasts.

TRANSITORY, a. Passing without continuance; continuing a short time; fleeting; speedily vanishing.

VALE, n. A tract of low ground, or of land between hills; a valley.

Key Scripture

Psa 103:15 — "As for man, his days are as grass: as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth."

Psa 103:16 — "For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone; and the place thereof shall know it no more."

Psa 103:17 — "But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him, and his righteousness unto children's children;"

Isa 40:8 — "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever."

Modern Corruption

The greatest Cistercian church in Wales, founded by a prince who died in its habit, and now a field.

expand to see more

The corruption is the confusion of permanence with significance — the builder's conviction that what endures in stone is what mattered. Owain Cyfeiliog was a poet as well as a prince and should have known better, and the order he joined had written the warning into its own statutes against ornament. The stones went to barns. What the psalm offers instead is not a smaller hope but a different one: “But the mercy of the LORD is from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him” (Psa 103:17).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the word of God, and not the work of God's servants, is what abides. “The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) is addressed to a people about to lose everything they had built, and it was enough for them. A congregation that loses a building has lost a building.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin strata, a paved way; Welsh ystrad, a vale; Hebrew chatsir (H2682), grass; Hebrew tsits (H6731), a flower; Hebrew chesed (H2617), covenant mercy.

expand to see more

Welsh ystrad — a vale or strath, Latinised as strata.

Hebrew chatsir (H2682) — grass, herbage; “his days are as grass” (Psa 103:15).

Hebrew tsits (H6731) — a blossom, a flower; “as a flower of the field, so he flourisheth” (Psa 103:15).

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath; “For the wind passeth over it, and it is gone” (Psa 103:16).

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — steadfast covenant mercy; “from everlasting to everlasting upon them that fear him” (Psa 103:17).

Usage

"“the place thereof shall know it no more” (Psa 103:16) — said over a field near Welshpool."

"“But the mercy of the LORD” (Psa 103:17) — the half that does not become pasture."

"“but the word of our God shall stand for ever” (Isa 40:8) — the only masonry that holds."
